entries.notes: Founded by Amos Hoff, Prof. of Physics — Phoenix College faculty since 1937.
Club-funded and ground 24" f7 telescope installed on the Phoenix College campus.
Telescope de-commissioned.
Incorporated as a 501(c)(3) non-profit. Newsletter: Sky-Lines.

New Cassegrain optics for the Amos Hoff 24" reflector, ground by optician Don Loomis, unveiled November 21. Members toured Lowell Observatory's Andrews Mesa site in October, viewing the 13" astrocamera used to discover Pluto.
Observatory proposed for Paradise Valley Park (near Paradise Valley Community College). Proposal denied; 24" mirror sold and installed in a private observatory near Alpine, AZ.

Bruce Lanard elected President, with Steve Coe — later a noted deep-sky observer and author — as Vice President. Dr. Arthur Hoag, Director of Lowell Observatory, spoke on current research programs including the Hubble constant.
New logo adopted.
Newsletter renamed PAStimes.
Meeting location changed.
Meeting location changed.
pasaz.org domain registered for email.
Website hosting at pasaz.org / geocities.com. Became a member of the Astronomical League.

PAS ran an Astronomy Day "Space Stations" event with NASA, the U.S. Geological Survey, Lowell Observatory, and the International Dark Sky Association, drawing hundreds of families for hands-on astronomy activities.
Mars made its closest approach to Earth in nearly 60,000 years; PAS set up 17+ telescopes for a packed public Mars-viewing event.
Meeting location changed.
PAS joined the Sally Ride Science Festival at ASU, offering solar viewing and handing out hundreds of donated Sky & Telescope magazines to encourage girls in science.
Meeting location changed.
Dr. Jeff Hester of ASU — imaging lead for the Hubble Space Telescope's iconic "Pillars of Creation" photograph — spoke at a special meeting.
Members voted to amend the club's constitution.
PAS officers called a special meeting to consider sponsoring a scale-model Solar System plaque on the PVCC campus.
PAS ran regular "dark sky" star parties at sites near Sedona/Cottonwood and Black Canyon City's High Desert Park, alongside public star parties at Paradise Valley Park.
University of Alberta physicist Dr. Don Page spoke on "Does God So Love the Multiverse?"
PAS opened a new dark-sky observing site, with the club funding a portable restroom for member star parties there.
ASU student and Mars Desert Research Station veteran Veronica Ann Zabala-Aliberto opened the season as guest speaker.
PAS members previewed ASU's inaugural Earth and Space Exploration Day at the October meeting.
PAS marked the 400th anniversary of Galileo's telescope discoveries with a lecture on NASA's planned Europa-Jupiter System Mission.
University of Arizona planetary scientist Richard Greenberg, author of "Unmasking Europa," spoke on the moon's icy surface.
PAS began organizing against CVEMS electronic billboards — like the one at Anthem Outlet Mall — as a growing threat to Arizona's dark skies.
Dr. David Williams previewed NASA's Mars Science Laboratory (Curiosity) rover, which launched later that month.
PAS covered the annular solar eclipse of May 20 with a dedicated special newsletter issue.
PAS covered the transit of Venus — an event that won't recur until 2117 — with a dedicated special newsletter issue.
PAS held its annual officer elections (Bruce Wurst elected President) and Awards Ceremony, including a youngest-member honor for Rockie Hervieux.
Retired chemist and longtime member Earl DeLong presented "The Chemistry of the Cosmos."
PAS held a silent auction of four original 1969 Life Magazine issues covering the Apollo 11 Moon landing, with proceeds benefiting the club.
Frequent PAS speaker Dr. David Williams of ASU was elected a Fellow of the Geological Society of America; asteroid 10,461 DAWilliams was named in his honor.
NASA's New Horizons became the first spacecraft to fly by Pluto — a world discovered from observations made at Arizona's Lowell Observatory — an event PAS tracked on its own club calendar.
WWII veteran and longtime member John C. Pulis passed away at 93; PAS had celebrated his 90th birthday with him in 2012.
Guest speaker Ted Blank shared that he moved to Arizona and joined PAS after attending the club's 2012 Venus Transit event as a visitor.
PAS's fight against light-pollution-causing electronic billboards scored a win with the legislature's defeat of HB 2507.
Five PAS members timed a stellar occultation by asteroid 113 Amalthea, contributing data toward determining the asteroid's size and shape.
Members experienced the "Great American" total solar eclipse and shared photos and videos at the following month's meeting.
Members proposed founding an Astrophotography Special Interest Group.
PAS celebrated its 70th anniversary with a special celebration event.
PAS's Annual Scholarship program was announced, organized by Sam Insana; James Arnold became its first recipient in early 2020.
Lowell Observatory historian Kevin Schindler spoke on the observatory's 125th "Quasquicentennial" anniversary.
PAS moved entirely to remote Zoom meetings during the COVID-19 pandemic, including its first virtual officer elections that May.
Longtime PAS speaker Klaus Brasch was honored by Lowell Observatory, which named asteroid 25226 Brasch for his volunteer service.
pasaz.org website redesigned on Google Sites.
Sam Insana — a beloved former PAS President and longtime leader of the club's outreach and occultation programs — passed away. The scholarship established the following year was named in his memory.
The Phoenix Astronomical Society / Sam Insana Memorial Scholarship established, honoring former PAS President Sam Insana.
Klaus Brasch surveyed "A Half Century of Astronomical Photography," tracing the technology's evolution from the era of the first daguerreotype of the Moon.
PAS held public viewing events for the year's annular "ring of fire" solar eclipse.
Members prepared for the total solar eclipse crossing North America — partial from Arizona — with safety reminders for observers and their families.
The newsletter's cover feature covered that month's total lunar eclipse, a "blood moon" visible across Arizona.
